Often
OF-n
adv.
From Middle English ofte, Anglo-Saxon oft: frequently, many times. Webster 1828: frequently; many times; not seldom. Malachi records what those who feared the LORD did often, and Christ tells Jerusalem how often He would have gathered her.

Biblical Definition

Malachi records a small and unofficial practice and then records heaven’s response to it: Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name (Malachi 3:16). In a chapter about a nation saying it is vain to serve God, a remnant simply talked to each other frequently, and a book was written. Our Lord uses the word in His lament over the city: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets... how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! (Matthew 23:37). Paul makes it the governing adverb of the Supper: as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come (1 Corinthians 11:26). And he writes to Timothy about a recurring bodily complaint with entirely practical counsel: use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities (1 Timothy 5:23).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OFTEN as frequently; many times; not seldom; and as an adjective in older usage, frequent, as in thine often infirmities.

expand to see more

OFTEN, adv. — Frequently; many times; not seldom.

OFTEN, a. (obsolete except in Scripture) — Frequent; as, thine often infirmities.

OFTENTIMES, adv. — Frequently; often; many times.

OFT, adv. — The older and shorter form, retained chiefly in poetry.

Anglo-Saxon oft, frequently.

Key Scripture

Malachi 3:16 — "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name."

Matthew 23:37 — "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!"

1 Corinthians 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

1 Timothy 5:23 — "Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities."

Modern Corruption

1 Timothy 5:23 is the standing embarrassment of teetotal absolutism, and Malachi 3:16 is the standing rebuke to the assumption that only organized ministry counts.

expand to see more

Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to use a little wine for his stomach and his frequent infirmities. The verse does not license drunkenness — Scripture condemns that repeatedly and requires elders not to be given to wine — but it does forbid the position that abstinence is itself a mark of holiness, since an apostle here prescribes the opposite to a young minister. The 1689 Confession’s teaching that God alone is Lord of the conscience applies directly: where Scripture has not bound, no man may bind. A believer may abstain for reasons of conscience, testimony, or the weakness of a brother, and Romans 14 protects him in it; what he may not do is make his abstinence the rule for others, which is precisely the reversal Romans 14 also forbids.

Malachi 3:16 is easy to pass over and is worth dwelling on. The chapter records a nation grown cynical — It is vain to serve God — and then a group who feared the LORD and simply spake often one to another. There is no programme, no office, no public act; there is frequent conversation among people who thought upon His name. The response is that the LORD hearkened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written. Where a church measures spiritual seriousness by attendance at organized events, this verse describes an activity it cannot count, and heaven wrote it down. The Puritan practice of conference — believers meeting to speak of the things of God — was a deliberate recovery of exactly this text.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew az with the frequentative sense, then... often; Greek posakis (G4212), how often; hosakis (G3740), as often as; puknos (G4437), frequent.

expand to see more

Greek posakis (G4212) — how often, how many times; the Lord’s lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).

Greek hosakis (G3740) — as often as, whenever; the governing adverb of the Supper (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Greek puknos (G4437) — frequent, often recurring; thine often infirmities (1 Timothy 5:23).

Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial or remembrance; a book of remembrance (Malachi 3:16).

Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear or revere; those who feared the LORD and spake often.

Usage

"They that feared the LORD spake often one to another (Malachi 3:16) — no programme and no office, and a book was written."

"How often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not! (Matthew 23:37) — the lament of a rejected Saviour."

"As often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup (1 Corinthians 11:26) — the Supper as a repeated showing forth."
